1.title: Get satellite alerts to the right people on the ground.
notes: About 2 minutes. The problem on the title slide: the Publisher is in the cloud, and Ground 1 and Ground 2 run in a separate environment. A static bridge carries alerts across that boundary.
The challenge is getting each event to the right ground system — Ground 1 or Ground 2 — on time, only to authorized systems, without building another custom link for every new consumer.
Event delivery from the Publisher, across the boundary, to Ground 1 and Ground 2.

Where do these events originate today, and where do the consumers that act on them run? How does an alert cross those environments today: a custom service, file transfer, or a manual step? Which separations are policy-driven, and which are network topology?

2.title: What we'll show today
notes: About 2 minutes. Three outcomes you will see today: controlled access, reliable delivery, and less custom integration.

Controlled access: only approved people and systems receive the alert. A permitted consumer receives an event; unpermitted publish or subscribe attempts are denied. Reliable delivery: important alerts wait when an operator or system is offline. A display may tolerate a missed live update; an operations workflow may not. A service goes down; queued alerts are delivered when it reconnects. Less custom integration: new recipients can be added with subscription and access-rule changes, leaving the producer unchanged. Connector, authentication, and topic-mapping setup still exist; the aim is to avoid another custom link for each consumer.
These three outcomes are what today's demo walks through.

What does on time mean for these consumers: seconds or minutes? Who approves which systems may see which events? Which consumers cannot tolerate a missed event? How long does onboarding a new consumer take today?

4.title: A satellite has an alert. A person on the ground needs it.
notes: About 2 minutes. The story on the slide: a satellite has an alert, a person on the ground needs it, and the seated operator reads Launch detected. Existing satellite communications stay in place; Solace starts after the feed is received.

Existing satellite communications and the ground link remain upstream. After the feed is received, the alert is delivered through a Solace Cloud broker, a static bridge across the boundary, and a ground broker, to the operator. Those two brokers and the bridge are the event mesh in this demo. Solace routes the alert to who needs it after the feed has been received.
Downstream event delivery after the received feed: from the cloud broker, across the static bridge, to the ground broker and the operator who needs the alert.

Does Solace replace the ground station or satellite link? No; it starts after the feed is received. Why two brokers instead of one? Cloud and ground are separate environments; the static bridge carries only allowed topics across that boundary. Why not send alerts point to point? That is the problem on slide 3; slide 7 shows a Kafka-plus-Solace path.

5.title: The right alert reaches the right people.
notes: About 2 minutes. A permitted operator receives Launch detected, and an unauthorized application is blocked.

Topics decide where an event goes. Access control decides who may publish or subscribe. A Solace topic is a string of levels in the message header, for example ssa/unclass/ground1/launch/25544/alert. The broker routes on the topic without reading the payload. Configuration covers queues, subscriptions, bridge subscriptions, and ACL profiles. ACL profiles have separate publish-topic and subscribe-topic controls, each a default action plus exceptions. Queue bind and consume permissions are reviewed separately.
Topic routing and broker-enforced publish and subscribe permissions on the same path.

Does the broker read the payload? No, it routes on the topic in the message header. Can it default to deny? Yes, each ACL profile has a default action plus exceptions for publish and subscribe topics. Where are permissions managed? On the broker: ACL profiles assigned to client usernames, so apps don't enforce it themselves.

8.title: What you will see, one step at a time
notes: About 1 minute on the map, then 5 to 10 minutes for the demo, returning to this map between demos. Events flow from the cloud broker to the ground broker, then to Ground 1 and Ground 2. The dashed line is the bridge: the ground side opens the connection outbound to the cloud. Two broker roles: a Solace Cloud service and a local software broker. The example topic is ssa/unclass/ground1/launch/25544/alert.
Demos 1–3 stand on their own. Click-by-click steps and recorded videos are in the repository Quick Reference.

A publisher sends events toward Ground 1 and Ground 2. The example topic ssa/unclass/ground1/launch/25544/alert has six labeled levels: root, classification, site, category, object, and event. Topic wildcards select which events reach each consumer. In Solace topic subscriptions, * by itself matches exactly one level — any single value at that position. For example, ssa/unclass/*/launch/> matches a launch from any ground site. A * can also follow a prefix at that same level; for example, ground* matches ground, ground1, and ground2. The > wildcard, used by itself at the end of a subscription, matches one or more remaining levels — everything after that point. For example, ssa/unclass/ground1/*/25544/> matches every event for object 25544 at Ground 1. Compare those two subscriptions: launches from any site versus every event for object 25544 at Ground 1. Each subscriber shows only matching events.
A restricted client may publish and subscribe on an allowed prefix and is refused on a denied prefix. The broker's response is visible on the page and in Broker Manager.

Send a guaranteed alert while a service is disconnected and the bridge stays up. The alert waits in a local durable queue and arrives tagged Queued when receiving resumes. A direct alert sent while disconnected does not appear after reconnect.

An observer agent watches the existing Publisher and Operators. The primary operator is disconnected, alerts are sent, then it reconnects. Asked 'What happened overnight to the primary operator? Was anything missed?', Operations Watch reports the outage window and the queued alerts that were delivered.
One topic path can serve different interests, enforce client permissions, and hold a guaranteed alert on a durable queue until the consumer is back.

Does * match more than one level? No. * matches a single level (either the whole level, or a prefix such as ground* at that level). > matches one or more trailing levels and only when it stands alone at the end. Who opens the bridge connection? The ground side connects outbound to the cloud, so no inbound port is needed on the ground. Is the AI needed for delivery? No; demos 1–3 stand alone.

9.title: De-risking Agent Mesh in federal environments
notes: About 3 minutes. Three federal AI-agent concerns, with proposed deployment controls and tests, after the core broker demo and Demo 4 (Operations Watch).

AI agent and data boundary: agents and data stay within the approved boundary. The boundary is the whole application — model, tools, external services, and storage — not only the model endpoint. Inventory outbound dependencies and verify actual data flows. Sensitive data and official records: conversations and generated files may be sensitive or may qualify as official records. Follow the customer-approved retention schedule, restrict access by designation or classification, and preserve legal holds with customer storage and records-management controls. Undo and conflicting changes: identify irreversible actions and require a human check before execution. Plan how to reverse or correct each action where possible, and test conflict handling and recovery after partial completion. Handling classified information would require an approved deployment with an Authorization to Operate (ATO) covering that classification level. This demonstration is unclassified.
Agent Mesh lets you add an observing agent on the same guaranteed path, with customer controls for boundary, records, and irreversible actions.

Can it run on a private or local model? Yes. Solace Agent Mesh supports configurable LLM endpoints, including custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints through LiteLLM and self-hosted options such as Ollama. Does the agent change anything? No. In Demo 4, Operations Watch only observes: it uses read-only SEMP and a Direct subscription, does not publish, and does not consume from the operator's queue. Delivery in demos 1–3 does not depend on it. What about classified data? Classified use needs an approved deployment with an ATO at that level. This demo is unclassified.

10.title: Prove the business value in your environment.
notes: About 2 minutes. A short, staged pilot that proves three results, reusing today's demo path as Stage 1.

The pilot is meant to prove three results. Controlled access: allowed and denied attempts match the permission plan. Evidence: a test log and denial counts in Broker Manager. Delivery: validate expected delivery in planned outage cases. Evidence: queue depth and delivery counts in Broker Manager and Insights. Integration: add a recipient via subscriptions and access rules, with no producer changes, and document federal feasibility findings. Broker Manager and Insights give built-in messaging-layer monitoring (queue depth, consumers, clients, rates) that many programs build by hand in Grafana; they don't replace Grafana for app or business metrics, and Solace can feed Grafana via SEMP or a Prometheus exporter. Stage 1 reuses today's demo. Later stages run in your approved environment.
A concrete way to connect controlled access, fewer missed important alerts, and less repeated integration effort to evidence in the customer's environment.

Does this replace our Grafana? No; Broker Manager and Insights cover the broker layer built in, and metrics can feed an existing Grafana via SEMP or a Prometheus exporter. Do producers change when we add a consumer? No; the new consumer gets a subscription and access rules. What does Stage 1 need? Reuse the demo path with the unclassified example.
